titre_video: Bond markets are falling apart now...

segments.titre: The bond safety rule has just broken
segments.resume: The video opens with the claim that the long-standing rule that government bonds protect investors when all else fails has broken. Pension funds, retirees and savers see supposedly safe assets losing value month after month. Officials say the worst has passed, but the yield-curve alarm has only moved into a new, harder-to-hear phase.
segments.texte: For decades, one rule stood firm as the bedrock of the financial world. If all else fails, government bonds protect you. Trillions of dollars rest on that single assumption. That rule just broke. The bond market is flashing red. Pension funds, retirees, and careful savers who did everything by the book are watching the supposedly safest assets on earth bleed, quietly, month after month, eating into their wealth. Meanwhile, the people in charge insist that the worst has passed, and they have a chart that seems to prove it. The bond market’s most reliable warning alarm has finally gone quiet, after the longest scream in modern history. Only the alarm didn’t stop because the danger passed. It clicked into a new phase, and this one is harder to hear. And much more concerning.

segments.titre: Why the bond market is the most consequential market
segments.resume: The bond market is less exciting than stocks or crypto but more important: global sovereign and corporate bonds hold about $109 trillion of debt, roughly 93 percent of world GDP. It sets the price of money and influences housing costs and everyday borrowing for an entire adult life.
segments.texte: So what exactly is breaking the world’s safest market, and why is nobody talking about what happens next? It might not be as exciting as the stock market or crypto, but the bond market is the most consequential financial market of all. Today the global sovereign and corporate bond markets hold around $109 trillion in debt, equivalent to roughly 93 percent of the world's annual economic output. It decides what you pay for a roof over your head, and it has quietly set the price of money for your entire adult life.

segments.titre: How bonds and yields work as the economy's thermostat
segments.resume: A government that spends more than it taxes sells IOUs to investors and promises repayment with interest, called the yield. The yield acts as the economy's thermostat, influencing mortgages, car finance, credit cards and savings rates, even though it never appears on a statement.
segments.texte: The mechanism is simple. When a government wants to spend more than it collects in tax, it doesn’t call a bank. It writes an IOU, sells it to investors around the world, and promises to pay it back later with interest. That interest is called the yield. It’s more than an incentive for people to buy bonds. It’s the thermostat of the whole economy. Your mortgage, your car finance, the interest on your credit card, and the rate on your savings can all be influenced by it. You’ll never see it on a statement, but it’s sitting prominently on the wall of every bank in the world.

segments.titre: Trust drives yields: the 2026 global repricing
segments.resume: When investors trust a government its yields stay low; when trust fades, yields climb because the state must pay more to attract lenders. The bond market's base price of money matters more than any stock wobble, and in 2026 it is repricing almost everywhere at once. The mortgage and savings sentence is repeated in the speech.
segments.texte: When investors trust a government, the yield on its bonds sits low. But when they stop trusting it, the yield climbs, because the government has to pay more to convince anyone to lend to it. That’s why the growing global bond market crisis outranks any single stock market wobble. This market is the base price of money. In 2026, it is repricing almost everywhere at once. Your mortgage, your car finance, the interest on your credit card, and the rate on your savings can all be influenced by it. Rent can be affected indirectly, too.

segments.titre: Zero rates and central bank bond buying after 2008 and 2020
segments.resume: After the 2008 financial crisis and the early 2020 pandemic, central banks cut rates to near or below zero and became major buyers of government debt. This produced an unusually long period of very low borrowing costs, with some short-term rates negative.
segments.texte: Now, this didn’t start recently, and it wasn’t caused by a single government. After the Great Financial Crisis of 2008, and again when the pandemic hit in early 2020, central banks needed to urgently stimulate their economies. So, they took an unprecedented step: They cut interest rates to almost zero, or even marginally below zero in some cases. Then, they took it a step further and became major buyers of government debt, purchasing large amounts to help keep borrowing costs low, regardless of the private sector’s appetite for taking on the risk. The result was an unusually prolonged period of very low borrowing costs. In some markets, short-term interest rates even fell below zero.

segments.titre: The free-money era: governments, companies and households borrow
segments.resume: With borrowing nearly free and buyers for any amount of debt, governments borrowed repeatedly. Large companies borrowed too, often sending the money back to shareholders through record buybacks, while ordinary people used cheap mortgages and car loans, inflating house prices. A generation came to believe money would always be cheap.
segments.texte: Imagine you run a country. Borrowing costs almost nothing, and a buyer turns up for any amount of debt you want to issue. What do you do? You borrow. Then you borrow again. Then you borrow a bit more, because there’s basically no charge, no angry phone call, and nobody carefully scrutinizing what the money is for before rubberstamping a loan. Of course, it wasn’t only governments taking advantage of the free money gravy train. The largest companies also borrowed massive amounts. But a great deal of it went straight back out to shareholders, in record share buybacks. Share prices went to the moon, and top executives were handsomely rewarded. Ordinary people also jumped on the free money train en masse. Why wouldn’t they? Cheap mortgages sent house prices vertical, and cheap car finance put flashier cars ever on the road. A whole generation grew up believing money was cheap and always would be. Everyone was getting richer, or at least so it seemed.

segments.titre: Global debt reaches $365.5 trillion
segments.resume: The Institute of International Finance counted global debt at $365.5 trillion in the first half of 2026, up more than $10 trillion in six months and about 310 percent of world output. That equals roughly $44,000 per person on Earth.
segments.texte: But in the background, behind the euphoria, the bill kept adding up. And it quietly grew into a monster. The Institute of International Finance counted global debt at $365.5 trillion in the first half of 2026. That’s an increase of more than $10 trillion in just six months, and worth around 310 percent of everything the world produces. Divide that across every person alive, and it’s roughly $44,000 each, man, woman, and child.

segments.titre: Borrowing accelerates: $29 trillion of bond issuance in 2026
segments.resume: Instead of braking, borrowing is accelerating: the OECD expects a record $29 trillion raised from bond markets in 2026, about $79 billion per day. Advanced economies now pay more interest on traded government debt than the world invests in AI, defense or clean energy.
segments.texte: Now, you would think that with global debt spiraling out of control, the people in control of the economic levers would have started pulling the handbrake. But the opposite has happened. Borrowing is not slowing; it’s accelerating. The OECD expects governments and companies to raise a record $29 trillion from bond markets in 2026. That works out at about $79 billion of fresh debt taken out of global capital markets every single day. To give you an idea of the staggering scale, the world’s advanced economies now pay more in interest on their traded government debt than the entire planet invests in artificial intelligence, defense, or clean energy.

segments.titre: Trump's golden age as a bar tab, and inflation as the cause
segments.resume: President Trump calls the current era a golden age, but the narrator argues that a golden age funded by borrowing is a bar tab that will come due. The bill arrives through inflation, which appears when the money supply grows faster than goods and services and prices rise.
segments.texte: President Donald Trump says the country has entered a “golden age”, and for some Americans at the top of the economic pile that may be true. But a golden age funded by borrowing isn’t really a golden age. It’s a bar tab with your name on it. And no matter how well you know the barkeeper, sooner or later that tab is going to come due. That’s exactly what’s happening now. And the reason is something that is typically the direct result of flooding economies with cheap, bountiful money: Inflation. When the amount of money in circulation grows faster than the amount of goods and services available to purchase with it, prices go up. And when they did, the lender stopped smiling.

segments.titre: Inflation makes lenders demand higher yields
segments.resume: Using a $100 loan and 10 percent inflation as an example, the narrator shows that lenders lose purchasing power and therefore demand proper compensation. Government yields climbed and have kept rising in fits and starts, breaking the quiet rule underpinning global financial security.
segments.texte: Think about what inflation does to anyone lending money. If I lend you a hundred dollars and prices rise 10 percent, the money you hand back buys less than what I gave up. I’ve lost money by being generous. Lenders are not in the business of being generous. So, they demanded to be paid properly again. The yield on government debt climbed, and it has kept climbing in fits and starts ever since. And that’s what broke the quiet rule

segments.titre: Long-dated Treasuries have lost about 60 percent since 2020
segments.resume: Government bonds were long the safe part of any portfolio, but since 2020 they have been among the most exposed. The Bank of America long-bond index of long-dated US Treasuries is down about 60 percent since 2020, to levels last seen in 2000, and a typical long-bond fund has lost nearly half, wiping out the conservative saver's promise.
segments.texte: underpinning global financial security. For generations, government bonds were the safe place in any portfolio, the asset class you moved into when you wanted to reduce your risks. But since 2020, that safe place has been one of the most exposed places to stand. The Bank of America’s long-bond index, which tracks long-dated U.S. Treasuries, has fallen about 60 percent since 2020, back to levels last seen in 2000. A typical long-bond fund has lost somewhat less, somewhere near half. Either way, long-term government bonds, often treated as low-risk assets, have delivered price losses on a scale usually associated with much riskier investments. For the conservative saver, that’s the entire promise of government bonds, gone. You did nothing wrong, and you followed the rules.

segments.titre: The biggest bond buyers are walking away
segments.resume: Central banks, foreign governments and private investors are the main buyers of government bonds. The Fed and ECB stopped replacing maturing bonds, the Bank of England sold outright, and foreign governments reduced reserves, leaving fussier private investors who demand higher returns for a record supply of debt, so yields rise.
segments.texte: Only the bedrock turned out to be sand. Faced with persistently falling prices, the biggest buyers of government bonds have done what you would expect them to do: They’ve been walking away. The biggest buyers of bonds typically fall into three categories: central banks, foreign governments, and private investors. Central banks represented the safety net. For years, they pretty much bought whatever was issued. And then they stopped. The Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank quit replacing the bonds that matured, and the Bank of England went further and sold outright. At the same time, foreign governments began reducing the reserves they used to park in U.S., British, and European debt. What’s left is the private investor class, and private investors are the fussiest of the three. They demand a higher price for taking the risk. Bottom line: there is more debt for sale than at any point in history, aimed at a smaller pool of buyers who want more in return. So, as you might expect, yields are rising in response.

segments.titre: Sovereign borrowing in 2026: $14.1 trillion, $5.3 trillion by the US
segments.resume: S&P estimates 143 rated sovereigns will borrow the equivalent of $14.1 trillion from long-term markets in 2026, almost 40 percent of it by the United States, which raises $5.3 trillion alone. Governments' need to sell bonds is not slowing despite rising costs, straining the financial system.
segments.texte: S&P estimates that 143 rated sovereign governments will borrow the equivalent of $14.1 trillion from long-term markets in 2026. Almost 40 percent of that is from one borrower: the U.S., raising $5.3 trillion on its own. So, there’s no slowing in governments’ need to sell bonds to finance their spending, despite the rising costs of doing so. The financial system is coming under increasing strain as a result. You can see it clearly in one crucial number.

segments.titre: The term premium hits its highest level since 2011
segments.resume: The term premium is the extra yield investors demand for locking money into long maturities of up to 30 years, or 50 years for the UK and France. The Federal Reserve's own measure for US Treasuries has risen to its highest level since 2011, meaning the US no longer borrows for free or cheaply.
segments.texte: The term premium. Bonds are issued with a wide variety of maturity dates – the date on which the government must repay the IOU. They range from a matter of weeks to 30 years, though some governments, including the U.K. and France, have sold bonds running out to 50 years. And obviously, bonds with longer maturity dates carry higher risk for investors. The term premium is the extra interest that investors demand for locking their money up for decades, when they can’t be sure what the deficits or the country will look like by the time they’re repaid. And it’s growing. With respect to U.S. Treasuries, the Federal Reserve’s own measure of the term premium has climbed to its highest level since 2011. The implication is clear. Investors are no longer lending to the safest borrower on earth for free, and they’re no longer doing it cheaply either.

segments.titre: US net interest costs exceed the defense budget
segments.resume: In fiscal 2025 the United States spent $970 billion on net interest, more than the $859 billion for national defense, making interest the third-largest federal budget item behind Social Security and Medicare. The CBO expects it eventually to become the largest line, buying nothing new.
segments.texte: And the U.S. is feeling it where it hurts most: in its pocket. In fiscal 2025, the United States spent $970 billion on net interest, more than the $859 billion it spent on national defense. Interest is now the third-largest item in the entire federal budget, behind Social Security and Medicare. And the Congressional Budget Office expects it to eventually pass Social Security and become the single biggest line of all. That money buys nothing. It doesn’t build a road, pay a teacher, or equip a soldier. It just keeps the old debt alive, and the cost has already reached the doorstep.

segments.titre: Mortgage rates at 7.40 percent add $367 a month
segments.resume: The average US 30-year mortgage rate was 7.40 percent in the week ending October 8, 2026, versus 6.30 percent a year earlier. On a $500,000 mortgage that adds about $367 a month, or more than $4,400 a year.
segments.texte: The average 30-year U.S. mortgage rate was 7.40 percent in the week ending October 8, 2026. A year earlier, it was 6.30 percent. It doesn’t seem like much. But on a $500,000 mortgage, that jump adds about $367 to the monthly payment, or more than $4,400 a year.

segments.titre: Japan, the yen carry trade and its heavy debt
segments.resume: Japan was for three decades the world's quietest lender: ultra-low domestic rates pushed banks, pension funds and households to invest in US Treasuries and European debt, the so-called yen carry trade. Japan's gross government debt is about 235 percent of GDP, which only didn't matter while rates sat on the floor.
segments.texte: But the consequences aren’t just constrained to the U.S. They’re felt around the world. To prove it, look no further than the country that stayed the calmest for the longest. Japan. For three decades, Japan was the world’s quietest lender. Its own rates were so low that in search of profits, Japanese banks, pension funds and households sent their money overseas, into U.S. Treasuries and European debt. That flow of capital, sometimes called the “Yen carry trade,” was one of the foundations the entire global system stood on. Japan is also one of the most heavily indebted major economies, with gross government debt at around 235% of GDP. Usually, that level of indebtedness in an advanced economy would give bond investors cause for concern. It simply didn’t matter while rates sat on the floor.

segments.titre: Japanese yields rise and investors sell US bonds
segments.resume: Japanese yields rose despite official efforts: the 10-year hit three percent on September 1, 2026, first since 1996, and the 30-year passed 4.2 percent in October. Japanese investors sold close to $30 billion of US debt in Q1 2026, the largest quarterly exit in four years, which raises US borrowing costs, from a Tokyo auction to an Ohio mortgage.
segments.texte: But in the background, the pressure inside the Japanese economy was building. Yields started rising, despite the Japanese authorities’ best efforts to control them. On September 1, 2026, the yield on 10-year Japanese government bonds touched three percent for the first time since 1996. The 30-year went on to a record above 4.2 percent in early October. The effects were predictable. Japanese investors started shedding U.S. bonds. Think about it. If a Japanese saver can finally earn a decent return at home, with no currency risk, why send the money across the Pacific to the U.S.? In the first three months of 2026, Japanese investors sold close to $30 billion of U.S. government debt, the biggest quarterly exit in four years. One of America’s most reliable lenders is quietly heading home. And when a big lender leaves, the borrower has to offer more to tempt somebody else in to take its place. That is how a bond auction in Tokyo ends up raising the cost of a mortgage in Ohio.

segments.titre: The Liz Truss gilt crisis of 2022
segments.resume: Britain already ran the experiment: in September 2022 Prime Minister Liz Truss announced £45 billion of unfunded tax cuts and the bond market revolted, sending gilt yields up and the pound to a record low. Leveraged pension funds were forced into spiral selling, the Bank of England promised £65 billion of emergency buying, and Truss left after 49 days, famously outlasted by a lettuce.
segments.texte: And once the cycle of rising yields starts, things can start unravelling rapidly. Britain already ran the experiment, and the world watched it live. In September 2022, new Prime Minister Liz Truss presented a budget with £45 billion of tax cuts, around $50 billion at the time, and no credible plan to pay for them. The bond market took one look and decided it didn’t believe a word of it. British government bond yields exploded. The pound fell to a record low. Pension funds that had borrowed against their own bonds were forced to sell more as prices fell, which pushed prices down further, in turn forcing more selling. The Bank of England had to promise an emergency £65 billion of bond buying to stop the whole system from collapsing. Truss was gone in 49 days, the shortest tenure of any British prime minister. A head of lettuce famously survived intact longer than that. We can laugh about the lettuce. But the fact is an unelected market removed an elected government in just seven weeks. Meanwhile, the issue never really went away. British borrowing costs are now higher than they were during that crisis.

segments.titre: UK borrowing costs now exceed the Truss crisis levels
segments.resume: The 30-year gilt rose above six percent in October 2026, its highest since 1998, and debt interest cost Britain £97.6 billion in 2025-26, the second-highest on record. Fitch says Britain's interest burden relative to revenue is about double the average top-rated sovereign, with no single villain this time, just a slow grind.
segments.texte: The 30-year gilt, as British government bonds are known, climbed above six percent in October 2026, its highest level since 1998. Debt interest alone cost Britain £97.6 billion in the 2025–26 financial year, the second-highest figure on record, according to the cited data. Fitch notes that Britain’s interest burden is about double that of the average top-rated sovereign relative to revenue. And this time there’s no reckless budget to blame and no villainous bankers to point the finger at. Just a slow grind that gets tighter every month.

segments.titre: France now borrows more expensively than Italy and Greece
segments.resume: France, once regarded as one of the safest borrowers, saw its yield gap over Germany widen in October 2026 to the largest since the 2011 eurozone debt crisis. It now borrows at higher cost than both Italy and Greece, turning the core of EU financial stability into the periphery.
segments.texte: But the UK is far from alone in struggling to contend with the consequences of rising bond yields. France has always been regarded as one of the safest borrowers on earth, a country where governments fell over the size of the debt rather than the other way around. Not anymore. In October 2026, the gap between what France pays to borrow and what Germany pays widened to its largest margin since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011. One comparison says it all. France is now borrowing more expensively than both Italy and Greece. The core of European Union financial stability has become the periphery.

segments.titre: French debt, political instability and the ECB backstop trap
segments.resume: France's debt is about 119 percent of GDP with a 5.4 percent deficit, and its interest bill of around €65 billion is the largest budget line. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu survived two no-confidence votes, the 2027 budget with €54 billion of savings faces a divided parliament, and rating agencies have downgraded or warned France. The ECB's tool to cap borrowing costs cannot be used because France is under the excessive deficit procedure.
segments.texte: France’s debt is about 119 percent of its economy, and its deficit is running at 5.4 percent. Its interest bill, around €65 billion (or about $72 billion) this year, is now the single biggest line in the national budget, ahead of both defense and education. Political instability has followed in its wake. In January 2026, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu [seh-bas-TYEN luh-KOR-noo] survived two no-confidence votes as the government sought to pass a budget through a divided parliament. The 2027 budget, carrying €54 billion of savings (or about $60 billion) went to the same divided house in October. The leading credit rating agencies, S&P, Moody’s and Fitch, have all marked France down or put it on notice, which is likely to make further borrowing even more expensive. There’s a trap inside the trap, too. The European Central Bank has a tool designed to cap a member’s borrowing costs, but it cannot legally use it on France, because France is already inside the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. The one backstop that exists is unavailable to the country that needs it.

segments.titre: The US owes over $40 trillion and mostly refinances old debt
segments.resume: The UK and France are a sideshow next to the US, the borrower that sets the price for everyone, which now owes over $40 trillion and spends more on debt service than on its military. Nearly 80 percent of projected 2026 OECD borrowing refinances existing debt, and US debt taken at near-zero rates is being refinanced at four to five percent. The average rate on outstanding Treasuries rose from 1.47 percent to about 3.5 percent. One sentence is duplicated in the speech.
segments.texte: But, large and structurally significant to the global economy as the UK and France may be, the growing bond crises in those nations are, to an extent, just a sideshow. The U.S. is the borrower that sets the price for everyone else, and it now owes more than $40 trillion. That number is too big to feel, so here are two that aren’t. The U.S. government spends more servicing its debt than it spends on its entire military. And nearly 80 percent of the borrowing projected for OECD governments in 2026 is expected to refinance existing debt. It’s old debt being refinanced at today’s prices. It’s old debt being refinanced at today’s prices. In the U.S., debts taken on when interest costs were close to zero are now being refinanced at around four to five percent. The average interest rate on outstanding Treasury securities has climbed to about 3.5 percent, from 1.47 percent five years ago.

segments.titre: The yield curve un-inverts, but recessions follow after
segments.resume: The yield curve inverted from July 2022 to September 2024, a record 792 days, and its un-inversion was read as good news. In recent cycles recessions began after the curve reverted rather than during inversion, with an average gap of about seven months in 1990, 2001 and 2007, so un-inversion does not mean the warning is over.
segments.texte: Which brings us back to the alarm that went quiet. For decades, economists watched one signal more closely than the rest to gauge the health of the bond markets. When the costs of short-term borrowing rise above long-term borrowing, the yield curve inverts, and a recession tends to follow. Picture a bank that charges you more for a two-year loan than for a 30-year mortgage. That is not business as usual. That is a warning. From July 2022 to September 2024, the curve stayed inverted for 792 days, the longest stretch in modern history. Then it un-inverted, and the headlines read it as good news, the economy returning to normal. But that’s a misleading read. In recent cycles, recessions haven’t begun while the curve is inverted. They’ve begun after it reverts. Historically, the gap between the un-inversion and the start of a recession averaged about seven months across the financial crises in 1990, 2001, and 2007. So, the yield curve un-inverting isn’t necessarily a signal that the warning is over. In some past cycles, recessions have begun after the curve reverted.

segments.titre: The vicious cycle: yields at 5.56 percent and a stale CBO forecast
segments.resume: Higher yields mean a bigger interest bill, more borrowing, more debt for sale and higher yields again. On October 13 the 30-year Treasury yielded 5.56 percent, with the 20-year slightly higher, and the 10-year was 5.21 percent. The CBO's forecast of an interest bill doubling to $2.1 trillion assumed a 10-year near four percent, so it is likely short by hundreds of billions of dollars.
segments.texte: The logic is simple, mathematical, and inescapable. Higher yields mean a bigger interest bill. And a bigger interest bill means more borrowing is needed, just to cover it. More borrowing means more debt for sale, into a market that is demanding more to buy it. Which in turn pushes yields higher again. It’s a vicious cycle, and it’s the same story at the long end of the curve as at the short. On October 13, the 30-year Treasury yielded 5.56 percent, and the 20-year, which should pay less because the lender is tying up the money for a shorter time, yielded slightly more. When the market charges a premium for the very longest loans, it is pricing doubt, not trust in growth. And the doubt seems to be growing. The Congressional Budget Office expects the U.S.’s interest bill to roughly double in the next decade, to around $2.1 trillion. But that forecast was built assuming the 10-year Treasury yield would sit near four percent. On October 13, it was 5.21 percent. In other words, unless the U.S. can somehow bring yields under control, that forecast is likely already short by hundreds of billions of dollars.

segments.titre: US Treasury buybacks fail to tame yields
segments.resume: The US, with Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, has fought the yield rise with little success. Doubling long-bond buybacks in August 2026 and tripling them in September brought only brief falls, and on October 8 a $22 billion 30-year auction cleared at 5.618 percent, the highest since August 2000, with foreign investors taking the largest share.
segments.texte: Now, as you can imagine, the U.S. hasn’t just been taking all of this lying down. It’s been actively fighting the yield explosion. However, so far, despite the many pronouncements to the contrary by the likes of Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, those efforts have met with little success. In August 2026, the U.S. Treasury announced it would at least double its buybacks of long-dated bonds. Yields fell. But just a day. Within weeks, the drop had been erased. Yields were climbing again. In September, the Treasury tripled its buyback program, and yields rose anyway. The market seems to have been expecting far more. Then, on October 8, the Treasury sold $22 billion of 30-year bonds at 5.618 percent, the highest yield on that bond since August 2000. The buyers did turn up, and foreign investors took the largest share. But they only turned up at a price the U.S. has not had to pay this century.

segments.titre: The Maldives: reserves drain and dollar withdrawal caps
segments.resume: The yield shock lands hardest on the weakest economies. The Maldives has debt near 127 percent of GDP and usable reserves of about $700 million by August 2026, around six weeks of imports. It tripled energy subsidies, its largest bank capped dollar withdrawals at $3,500 a month from October 1, and Fitch rates it deep junk with market access prohibitively expensive.
segments.texte: It’s tempting to read all of this as an American story, or a developed world one. It isn’t. It lands hardest on the countries with the least capacity to absorb it. Take the Maldives. Its debt is now around 127 percent of its GDP, and by August 2026 its usable foreign reserves had fallen to roughly $700 million, about a month and a half of imports. The country imports every drop of its fuel, so when prices spiked, it tripled its energy subsidies. To defend the currency peg, its largest bank capped dollar cash withdrawals at $3,500 a month from October 1. A tourist economy running out of dollars is not an abstraction. It’s a queue at the bank. The country can’t even borrow its way out. Fitch rates the Maldives deep in junk territory, and says market access is “prohibitively expensive.”

segments.titre: Bolivia and why poor borrowers pay first
segments.resume: Bolivia received a $1.9 billion IMF loan on October 2, 2026 after ending its diesel subsidy, which raised pump prices 83 percent overnight, lifted some bus fares up to 125 percent and led to a state of exception. Neither Bolivia nor the Maldives is reckless; expensive money hits the poorest borrowers first.
segments.texte: Or take Bolivia. On October 2, 2026, the IMF approved a $1.9 billion loan. Weeks earlier, the government had ended its diesel subsidy, and the price at the pump had jumped 83 percent overnight. Intercity bus fares rose by as much as 125 percent on some routes, and the country declared a state of exception to keep the roads open. Neither government is particularly reckless. Both are simply being forced to pay more for money in a world where a rich country can outbid them for every dollar. When money gets expensive,

segments.titre: Wealth concentration and asset inflation in the US
segments.resume: The crisis does not affect everyone equally: in Q2 2026 the top one percent of US households held a record 32.5 percent of wealth, the top tenth 68.9 percent and the bottom half 2.3 percent. Since 2019 the S&P 500 returned about 160 percent and US house prices rose about 50 percent, as cheap money inflated asset prices, with the richest tenth owning 87 percent of shares.
segments.texte: it gets expensive for the poorest borrowers first. And that brings us to arguably the most alarming part of this story, which almost nobody with a microphone will tell you, because almost everyone with a microphone is standing on the right side of it. This crisis isn’t affecting everyone equally. Its effects can widen the gap between lower-income households and the wealthiest. In the second quarter of 2026, the wealthiest one percent of U.S. households held a record 32.5 percent of all household wealth. The top tenth held 68.9 percent. The bottom half of households held just 2.3 percent. That concentration has been building for years, but it’s been accelerating in the last few. The S&P 500 has returned about 160 percent since the end of 2019, and house prices in the U.S. are up somewhere near 50 percent. Those fortunate to own assets have watched their prices inflate, largely because, as noted earlier, the same cheap money that built the debt pile also pushed the prices of everything up – groceries and assets. The richest tenth of Americans own 87 percent of the shares.

segments.titre: Falling real wages and rising household financial stress
segments.resume: Real average hourly earnings are up only about 2.6 percent since early 2020 and turned negative in September 2026, falling 0.7 percent against 3.7 percent inflation, with energy up over 20 percent and gasoline over 30 percent. 12.8 percent of credit card balances were 90 or more days past due in Q2 2026, only 47 percent of Americans could cover a $1,000 emergency, and the saving rate fell to 2.6 percent.
segments.texte: Now go to the bottom. Real average hourly earnings, what a paycheck actually buys, are up about 2.6 percent since early 2020, well below price inflation over the same period. In September 2026, they turned negative, falling 0.7 percent while prices rose 3.7 percent. Energy costs were up more than 20 percent on the year. Gasoline, more than 30. And it’s starting to bite. Hard. Among U.S. credit card balances, 12.8 percent were at least 90 days past due in the second quarter of 2026, up from 7.6 percent in late 2022 and approaching levels seen during the 2008 global financial crisis. Only 47 percent of Americans say they could cover a $1,000 emergency from cash. The personal saving rate fell to 2.6 percent in April 2026, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

segments.titre: The K-shaped economy: asset owners vs everyone else
segments.resume: The economy is described as K-shaped: the top arm climbs on inflating assets while the bottom arm falls under costs rising faster than wages. Asset owners have been paid for the debt, while others pay through rent, fuel and groceries, and commentators who call the economy fine are standing on the top arm.
segments.texte: Put the two halves together, and the real shape of the economy is revealed. Not a rising tide, and not a falling one. A K-shape. The top arm climbs, carried by assets that inflate. The bottom arm drops, dragged by costs that keep rising faster than wages. And the gap between them is where the debt is quietly being paid. If you own assets, you have, to an extent, been paid for your trouble. If you don’t, you have been paying for it, in rent, in fuel, in groceries, and in a wage that stopped keeping up before the pandemic even ended. The commentators who tell you the economy is fine are, almost without exception, standing on the top arm. Perhaps they aren’t feeling the pain, or perhaps they’re turning a blind eye to it.

segments.titre: Conclusion: the market prices doubt and everyone keeps paying more
segments.resume: Nobody knows how this ends: the bond market cannot be voted against, negotiated with or shamed, and it is pricing a world that has borrowed more than it can carry at rates once thought gone. After 15 years of assuming buyers would always appear, in 2026 patience and trust ran out. There is no workable plan to control yields or inflation, so everyone will keep paying more.
segments.texte: Nobody knows how this ends. The bond market is not something you can vote against, negotiate with, or shame into changing its mind. It prices what it sees, and right now it is pricing a world that has borrowed more than it can comfortably carry, at rates that were never supposed to come back. For 15 years, governments and investors both behaved as though the buyers would always turn up. In 2026, that stopped being true. Not because the money ran out, but because the patience and trust did. At the moment, there doesn’t seem to be a workable plan on the table to bring either bond yields or the rising inflation they’re contributing to under control. But until someone comes up with one, the only thing that does seem certain is that we’ll all just keep paying more.
